note: Two- or three-sentence summaries written for the atlas from the lead of each place's English Wikipedia article (linked as a source on the page). Nothing is added beyond what that lead says.

summaries.Q2914712: A Victorian-themed hotel and spa at Walt Disney World, opened in June 1988 as the Grand Floridian Beach Resort and renamed in 1997. Its 867 rooms are spread across six buildings, and it is considered Disney's flagship resort.
summaries.Q161562: Caltech is a private research university in Pasadena devoted to pure and applied science. It began in 1891 as a preparatory and vocational school founded by Amos G. Throop, took its present name in 1920, and still manages NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.
summaries.Q180402: A national park in California's Sierra Nevada, known worldwide for its granite cliffs, waterfalls, giant sequoia groves and meadows. It covers about 1,187 square miles across four counties, almost all of it designated wilderness, and became a World Heritage Site in 1984.
summaries.Q8731: The main international airport for Los Angeles, in the Westchester neighborhood about 18 miles southwest of downtown. Run by Los Angeles World Airports, it covers 3,500 acres with four parallel runways and handled more than 75 million passengers in 2023.
summaries.Q459096: The main airport of the Dallas–Fort Worth region, between the two cities. It is American Airlines' largest hub, and in 2022 and 2023 it ranked second in the world by passenger traffic, according to Airports Council International.
summaries.Q242111: A desert national park straddling the California–Nevada border, east of the Sierra Nevada, with salt flats, sand dunes, badlands, canyons and mountains. It is the largest national park in the contiguous U.S. and the hottest, driest and lowest; Badwater Basin lies 282 feet below sea level.
summaries.Q152660: A national park in the southern Sierra Nevada, east of Visalia, established on September 25, 1890. Its 404,000 acres of forested mountains include Mount Whitney, the highest point in the contiguous U.S., and the General Sherman Tree, the largest tree on Earth by volume.
summaries.Q735202: A desert national park in southeastern California, named for the Joshua trees that grow there. First declared a national monument in 1936, it became a national park in 1994 and covers about 795,000 acres, more than half of it wilderness.
summaries.Q1427197: A national park in West Texas on the border with Mexico, named for a great bend in the Rio Grande. It is the largest protected area of Chihuahuan Desert in the U.S., contains the Chisos Mountains, and shelters more than 1,200 plant and 450 bird species.
summaries.Q191824: A group of one national park and three California state parks on the far north coast, managed together. They protect about 45 percent of the old-growth coast redwood forest that remains, along with 37 miles of coastline.
summaries.Q676206: A national park in southeastern Arizona made up of two districts, one west and one east of Tucson. Both protect Sonoran Desert landscapes and wildlife, including the giant saguaro cactus; the eastern Rincon Mountains rise higher and are wetter than the western Tucson Mountains.
summaries.Q1143655: A remote national park about 68 miles west of Key West, reachable only by seaplane or boat. It protects the Dry Tortugas islands, coral reefs, shipwrecks and Fort Jefferson, an unfinished brick fortress built of more than 16 million bricks.
summaries.Q832945: A gold-rush ghost town in the Bodie Hills east of the Sierra Nevada, at about 8,400 feet. It boomed from 1876, reaching around 8,000 people by 1879, then faded; since 1962 it has been preserved as Bodie State Historic Park, visited by about 200,000 people a year.
summaries.Q965731: A research institute and natural history museum in San Francisco's Golden Gate Park, with more than 46 million specimens. Founded in 1853 as a learned society, it still does original research; its main building was completely rebuilt in 2008.
summaries.Q1559342: A historic hotel at 7000 Hollywood Boulevard in the Hollywood district of Los Angeles, also known as Hotel Roosevelt.
summaries.Q982241: A former mining district near the Rio Grande in far southwestern Texas. The discovery of cinnabar, the ore of mercury, in the mid-1880s drew some 2,000 people; today a ghost town of the old Chisos Mining Company remains, and about 78 people lived there in 2020.
summaries.Q1946237: A marine-life theme park in San Diego's Mission Bay Park, opened in 1964 as the first SeaWorld. It combines an oceanarium, public aquarium and animal rescue center, and is owned by United Parks & Resorts.
summaries.Q458547: A tiny Mojave Desert settlement on historic Route 66, west of Needles. In 2020 it still had a post office, a historic restaurant-motel and a Route 66 shop run by four residents; by 2024 only the gas station was open.
summaries.Q595439: A large pier at the foot of Colorado Avenue in Santa Monica, with a small amusement park, food stands, fishing spots and views out over the ocean. It is part of the Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area.
summaries.Q1972924: A concrete arch-gravity dam on the Sacramento River at the north end of the Sacramento Valley. At 602 feet it is the eighth-tallest dam in the U.S., and it holds back Shasta Lake, California's largest reservoir, for water storage, flood control and hydropower.
summaries.Q526354: A former silver-mining town in the Calico Mountains of the Mojave Desert, founded in 1881 and now a county park off Interstate 15 near Barstow. Walter Knott bought it in the 1950s and rebuilt most of it to look as it did in the 1880s.
summaries.Q1207585: A 57-acre amusement park in Buena Park that grew from Walter Knott's roadside berry stand of the 1920s; it officially opened under its current name in 1947. Now owned by Six Flags, it has more than 40 rides and attractions, including ten roller coasters.
summaries.Q1631096: A historic beachfront hotel in Coronado, across the bay from San Diego, and a rare surviving wooden Victorian beach resort. When it opened in 1888 it was the largest resort hotel in the world; it became a National Historic Landmark in 1977.
summaries.Q2074361: A 212-acre amusement park in Arlington, between Dallas and Fort Worth, and the first park in the Six Flags chain. It opened on August 5, 1961, after a year of construction funded by developer Angus G. Wynne Jr.
summaries.Q2276588: A theme park in Carlsbad, north of San Diego, opened on March 20, 1999, as the first Legoland outside Europe. It has more than 60 rides, shows and attractions, plus a water park, an aquarium and two hotels.
summaries.Q617891: The second Franciscan mission in the Californias, founded in San Diego on July 16, 1769, by Junípero Serra in land long inhabited by the Kumeyaay people. The present church, built in the early 1800s, is the fifth on the site, which is a National Historic Landmark.
summaries.Q1435790: A luxury hotel on Collins Avenue in Miami Beach, designed by Morris Lapidus and opened in 1954. In 2012 the Florida chapter of the American Institute of Architects put it first on its list 'Florida Architecture: 100 Years. 100 Places'.
summaries.Q646122: A family resort in Winter Haven built on the site of the former Cypress Gardens theme park, whose botanical gardens it kept. It includes the Legoland theme park, a water park, three places to stay and a separate Peppa Pig park opened in 2022.
summaries.Q101094405: The oldest masonry fort in the continental United States, on Matanzas Bay in St. Augustine. Spain began building it of coquina stone in 1672, after an English raid destroyed much of the town, and finished its core in 1695.
summaries.Q849039: A tiny unincorporated town 13 miles from Fredericksburg in the Texas Hill Country, named for the son of an early German settler. It is known for country music and its German-Texan heritage.
summaries.Q6411977: The largest ranch in the United States, about 825,000 acres of South Texas between Corpus Christi and Brownsville. Founded in 1853 by Captain Richard King and Gideon K. Lewis, it is mainly a cattle ranch and became a National Historic Landmark in 1961.
summaries.Q3109025: The world's largest developed geothermal field, in the Mayacamas Mountains about 72 miles north of San Francisco. Its 18 power plants draw steam from more than 350 wells; in 2019 they produced about a fifth of California's renewable energy.
summaries.Q3062422: An aerospace museum in Tucson with nearly 400 aircraft displayed across about 80 acres. It has also housed the Arizona Aviation Hall of Fame since 1991.
summaries.Q1413807: A Spanish mission in Santa Barbara, often called the 'Queen of the Missions', founded on December 4, 1786, as the tenth of California's missions. Like the others, it was built to strengthen Spain's claim to Alta California and to convert the local Chumash people.
summaries.Q7193314: A lighthouse on Highway 1 south of Pescadero, built in 1871 to guide ships along the Pacific coast. Its 115-foot white masonry tower ties as the tallest lighthouse on the West Coast, and it is still an active Coast Guard aid to navigation.
summaries.Q979378: A dam on the Salt River northeast of Phoenix, built between 1905 and 1911 and named for President Theodore Roosevelt. At 357 feet high it forms Theodore Roosevelt Lake, mainly for irrigation, water supply and flood control.
summaries.Q1128074: A former territorial prison in Yuma that held inmates from July 1, 1876, until it closed on September 15, 1909. Arizona State Parks now runs it as a museum, Yuma Territorial Prison State Historic Park.
summaries.Q2689743: A Spanish mission at the mouth of the Carmel River, first built in 1771 and among the most faithfully restored in California. From 1770 to 1833 it was the headquarters of all the Alta California missions, and Junípero Serra led it until his death in 1784.
summaries.Q1939057: A Spanish mission in San Juan Capistrano, founded on November 1, 1776, by Franciscan missionaries and named for Saint John of Capistrano. Secularized in 1833 and returned to the Catholic Church in 1865, it has been restored since about 1910 and is now a museum.
summaries.Q139063: A ghost town in the Mojave Desert in San Bernardino County, California.
summaries.Q3378203: A lighthouse at the south end of Key Biscayne, built in 1825 to guide ships past the Florida Reef. It was retired in 1878 when the Fowey Rocks light replaced it, served again from 1978 to 1990, and has stood within Bill Baggs Cape Florida State Park since 1966.
summaries.Q3141392: An upscale mall and mixed-use development in Houston's Uptown District, with office towers, two Westin hotels and about 400 stores. Its anchors include Macy's, Nordstrom, Neiman Marcus and Saks Fifth Avenue, across some 3 million square feet.
summaries.Q779685: A lighthouse on Point Reyes in Point Reyes National Seashore, overlooking the Gulf of the Farallones. Visitors can climb down about 300 steps to reach it, weather permitting, and a visitor center nearby covers the lighthouse and the park's marine life.
summaries.Q2159261: A former Harvey House hotel on the South Rim of the Grand Canyon, opened in 1905 and designed by Santa Fe Railway architect Charles Whittlesey. It stands near the railway's Grand Canyon Depot, at the northern end of the Grand Canyon Railway.
summaries.Q979133: A historic resort in Phoenix near 24th Street and Camelback Road, designed by Albert Chase McArthur and opened on February 23, 1929. Clark Gable and Carole Lombard often stayed there, and the Tequila Sunrise cocktail was invented at its bar.
summaries.Q5582298: Known as The Oldest House, this historic house museum at 14 St. Francis Street dates to about 1723 and is thought to be the oldest surviving house in St. Augustine. It shows the city's Spanish colonial building style with later English changes and is a National Historic Landmark.
summaries.Q7587188: A working lighthouse at the north end of Anastasia Island, built between 1871 and 1874 and still maintained as an active aid to navigation. It replaced Florida's first lighthouse, lit here in 1824, and keeps its original first-order Fresnel lens.
summaries.Q7207966: A historic lighthouse in Port Bolivar, built in 1872 and retired in 1933 after 61 years of service. It replaced an 1852 cast-iron tower that was pulled down during the Civil War so Union warships could not use it.
summaries.Q6816982: A historic hotel in downtown San Antonio, on ground that was part of the Battle of the Alamo. It is a contributing building in the Alamo Plaza Historic District, listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1977.
summaries.Q3472599: An oceanfront amusement park in Santa Cruz, founded in 1907. It is California's oldest surviving amusement park and one of the few seaside parks left on the West Coast.
summaries.Q5435793: A permanent market of food stalls, sit-down eateries and grocers at Fairfax Avenue and 3rd Street in Los Angeles, open seven days a week. It first opened in 1934, has more than 100 vendors, and has been a city Historic-Cultural Monument since 1991.
summaries.Q7738393: A retail and entertainment complex built on part of the historic Farmers Market in Los Angeles. It is owned by Caruso, the real estate company of Rick Caruso.
summaries.Q1687755: An Arizona state park in the old mining town of Jerome, centered on the Douglas Mansion, built in 1916 by a family of mining entrepreneurs. The mansion now houses a museum.
summaries.Q85761246: A science museum and planetarium of the University of Arizona in Tucson, named for author Grace Flandrau. Its Eos Planetarium Theater has a 15-meter dome and 146 seats, and its exhibits focus on Earth and space science.
summaries.Q4915840: A historic theater in Tombstone that operated on and off from December 1881 into the 1890s, closing as the silver mines shut down. From 1934 the building was leased as a coffee shop.
summaries.Q7241535: A Spanish fort built near the San Antonio River, founded on May 5, 1718, by Martín de Alarcón and 35 soldiers. It protected the mission of San Antonio de Valero and the soldiers' settlement, the first Spanish settlement in what became San Antonio.
summaries.Q3077790: A 19th-century U.S. Army post near Willcox in southeastern Arizona, founded in 1862 by California Volunteers after clashes with the Chiricahua Apaches, including the Battle of Apache Pass. Its remains are protected as Fort Bowie National Historic Site.
summaries.Q7241536: A fortress built by the Spanish Army in 1752 at the site of present-day Tubac, in southern Arizona. Its ruins are preserved in Tubac Presidio State Historic Park.
summaries.Q5307819: A Romanesque-style hotel completed in 1886 by cattleman Jesse Driskill, now the oldest operating hotel in Austin. It has been listed on the National Register of Historic Places since 1969 and has been run by Hyatt since 2013.
summaries.Q6842960: A café, souvenir and antique shop on Route 66 in Adrian, Texas, which bills itself as the halfway point between Los Angeles and Chicago, 1,139 miles from each end. A former owner, Fran Houser, inspired the character Flo in the movie Cars.
summaries.Q7862894: An Art Deco gas station and café built in 1936 on Route 66 in Shamrock, Texas, designed by J. C. Berry. Its two flared towers, glazed tile walls and neon accents make it an unusual example of the style on a roadside building.
summaries.Q14683250: A 928-foot pier at the end of Manhattan Beach Boulevard, with an octagonal building at its tip that houses the Roundhouse Aquarium. It is popular for fishing, surfing below and sunsets, and has a Volleyball Walk of Fame.
summaries.Q199359: A city-owned stadium in Orlando's West Lakes neighborhood, opened in 1936 as Orlando Stadium and later known as the Tangerine Bowl and the Florida Citrus Bowl. It hosts the Citrus Bowl, the Cure Bowl and the Pop-Tarts Bowl, plus the annual Florida Classic college game.
summaries.Q16846942: A soccer-specific stadium on West Church Street in Orlando's Parramore neighborhood, opened in 2017. It is home to Orlando City SC of Major League Soccer and the Orlando Pride of the National Women's Soccer League.
summaries.Q1324340: The first theme park at Walt Disney World, opened on October 1, 1971, and modeled after Disneyland in California. Its icon is Cinderella Castle, and in 2025 it welcomed 17.8 million visitors.
summaries.Q1052042: The second theme park at Walt Disney World, opened on October 1, 1982, as EPCOT Center and often described as a permanent world's fair. It celebrates technology and international culture, and its landmark is Spaceship Earth, a giant geodesic sphere.
summaries.Q764186: A zoological theme park at Walt Disney World, themed around the natural world and home to hundreds of live animal exhibits. Covering 580 acres, it was the largest theme park in the world when it opened.
summaries.Q1345090: A theme park at Walt Disney World, opened on May 1, 1989, as the Disney-MGM Studios. Its 135 acres are themed to an idealized Hollywood and to the worlds of film, television, music and theater.
summaries.Q597631: A commercial airport in Sanford, north of Orlando, built as Naval Air Station Sanford and used by the Navy until 1969. It serves as a secondary airport for the Orlando area, with lower fees than Orlando International.
summaries.Q1880820: The first park at Universal Orlando Resort, opened on June 7, 1990, with rides, shows and attractions themed to movies and television. It was later joined by Islands of Adventure, Volcano Bay and Epic Universe.
summaries.Q2583112: A theme park at Universal Orlando Resort that opened on May 28, 1999, alongside Universal CityWalk. Its opening turned Universal's Orlando site into a full resort.
summaries.Q2125296: A shopping, dining and entertainment district at Walt Disney World in Lake Buena Vista, first opened on March 22, 1975, as the Lake Buena Vista Shopping Village. Renamed several times, it became Disney Springs in 2015 and covers 120 acres in four areas.
summaries.Q66085108: The fourth theme park at Universal Orlando Resort, opened on May 22, 2025, a few miles south of the other parks. Its five themed areas include Super Nintendo World, How to Train Your Dragon – Isle of Berk and The Wizarding World of Harry Potter – Ministry of Magic.
summaries.Q2915574: A water park at Walt Disney World, opened on June 1, 1989, with one of the world's largest outdoor wave pools, big enough for bodysurfing. It is themed to the legend of a typhoon that scattered ships and surfboards across a tropical island.
summaries.Q3046174: A sports complex of about 230 acres at Walt Disney World, opened on March 28, 1997. Its nine venues host professional and amateur events all year, so families can pair tournaments with a vacation.
summaries.Q884556: A water park at Walt Disney World, opened on April 1, 1995, as the resort's third water park. Its water is heated to about 80 °F, and in 2016 it drew about 2.1 million guests.
summaries.Q2164222: A private liberal arts college in Winter Park, founded in 1885, making it Florida's oldest private university. It has about 3,000 students.
summaries.Q5508130: A private for-profit university in Winter Park that began as a recording studio in Dayton, Ohio, and moved to Florida in 1980. It teaches audio, design, computer animation and business, and became a university in 2008.
summaries.Q2564594: The nickname for sound stages at Universal Studios Florida where the wrestling promotion TNA taped its weekly show Impact! for much of its first two decades. The studio's stages have hosted wrestling productions since the 1990s.
summaries.Q2908501: A pavilion and aquarium in the World Nature area of EPCOT, themed as an ocean research base. With 5.7 million gallons of tanks it is the second-largest aquarium in the U.S., and it includes a ride, Turtle Talk with Crush and the Coral Reef Restaurant.
summaries.Q3030278: A value-category hotel at Walt Disney World near Animal Kingdom, with 1,920 rooms. It is decorated with oversized icons from Disney films, such as Herbie from The Love Bug and the puppies from One Hundred and One Dalmatians.
summaries.Q3030310: A moderate-category resort hotel at Walt Disney World, opened on August 1, 1997, in the Animal Kingdom resort area. Its theme draws on Spanish colonial and southwestern American style, and it was Disney's first moderate resort with a convention center.
summaries.Q2925356: The football stadium on the University of Central Florida's main campus, home of the UCF Knights. Opened in 2007, it has also hosted the Cure Bowl and the Hula Bowl.
summaries.Q6516447: A public airport owned by the City of Leesburg, three miles northeast of the city's downtown in Lake County.
summaries.Q455153: Florida's fourth-largest lake, about 15 miles northwest of Orlando. It is fed by a spring, rain and runoff, drains through a chain of lakes to the Ocklawaha River, and is ringed by parks and trails such as the Lake Apopka Wildlife Drive.
summaries.Q3214981: A large lake about 15 miles east of Lake Wales, almost entirely in Osceola County. Lake Kissimmee State Park on its shore is rich in wildlife, from bald eagles to sandhill cranes, and has a 'cow camp' about Florida cowboys of the 1870s.
summaries.Q7103029: Orlando's historic train station, built in 1926, about a mile south of downtown near the Orlando Health campus. It is served by Amtrak's Silver Meteor and Floridian, by SunRail commuter trains and by local and intercity buses.
summaries.Q7106371: A sports venue in Kissimmee at Osceola Heritage Park, part of Orlando City SC's training ground. Originally a baseball park for minor-league teams such as the Osceola Astros, it was converted in 2019 into a soccer stadium for the club's reserve team.
summaries.Q3030338: A value-priced resort at Walt Disney World, opened on December 14, 2003, and themed to 20th-century American pop culture. The second half of its original plan was halted after the September 11 attacks and later became the Art of Animation Resort.
summaries.Q3030345: A Disney Vacation Club resort in Lake Buena Vista, opened on May 17, 2004, on the former site of the Disney Institute and inspired by Saratoga Springs, New York. Spread over 65 acres, it is the largest Disney Vacation Club resort.
summaries.Q2919757: One of Walt Disney World's two original hotels, opened on October 1, 1971, with a South Seas theme. Designed by Welton Becket and Associates, it opened with 492 rooms and has been expanded three times since.
summaries.Q3030298: A New England-style resort on Crescent Lake in the EPCOT area of Walt Disney World, opened on November 19, 1990. It shares staff and amenities with its sister, the Yacht Club Resort, and includes Disney Vacation Club villas.
summaries.Q3030306: A moderate-category resort in the EPCOT area of Walt Disney World, close to the Typhoon Lagoon water park. It opened on October 1, 1988.
summaries.Q3030279: A value-category hotel at Walt Disney World near Animal Kingdom, with 1,412 rooms and 192 family suites, the first such suites at a Disney value resort. It is decorated with oversized icons of musical genres from Broadway to jazz.
summaries.Q3030299: A hotel and entertainment complex on Crescent Lake between EPCOT and Disney's Hollywood Studios, opened in 1996. The inn, the Atlantic Dance Hall and other parts of the boardwalk were designed by Robert A.M. Stern Architects.
summaries.Q20979434: A tropical-themed water park at Universal Orlando Resort, opened on May 25, 2017, as the first water park designed by Universal Creative. At its center stands Krakatau, a 200-foot volcano, with water coasters and capsule plunge slides.
summaries.Q3409012: A resort hotel between EPCOT and Disney's Hollywood Studios, opened on June 4, 1990, and run by Marriott rather than Disney. It and its sister hotel, the Swan, were designed by Michael Graves and are linked by a covered walkway across a lagoon.
summaries.Q2919960: One of Walt Disney World's two original hotels, opened on October 1, 1971, beside Magic Kingdom. It is a deluxe resort, recognizable by its A-frame main building.
summaries.Q3030286: A sports-themed value resort in the southern, Osceola County part of Walt Disney World. Like Disney's other value resorts, it is decorated with giant novelty icons.
summaries.Q3030352: A New England nautical-themed resort in the EPCOT area of Walt Disney World, opened on November 5, 1990, and designed by Robert A.M. Stern Architects. It sits beside its sister, the Beach Club, across Crescent Lake from the BoardWalk.
summaries.Q7099553: The main public convention center of Central Florida, at the south end of International Drive, opened in 1983. With about 7 million square feet, including 2.1 million of exhibit space, it is the second-largest convention center in the U.S., after Chicago's McCormick Place.
summaries.Q6417209: Kissimmee's train station, opened in 1883 and served by SunRail commuter trains and Amtrak's Floridian and Silver Meteor. It is the closest Amtrak station to Walt Disney World.
summaries.Q8026304: Winter Park's train station, built in 2014 when SunRail service began, on a line where stations have stood since 1882. It is served by SunRail and Amtrak, and is SunRail's second-busiest station.
summaries.Q2920554: A 7,500-seat baseball stadium at the ESPN Wide World of Sports Complex, built in 1997 and designed by David M. Schwarz. Its yellow stucco, green tile roofs, towers and arches mix Venetian Gothic, Mediterranean and Spanish influences.
summaries.Q1228570: A theme park in Orlando, sister to SeaWorld Orlando and Aquatica, where visitors can get close to marine animals such as bottlenose dolphins. It is owned by United Parks & Resorts.
summaries.Q3850035: The Central Florida ranching operations of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, about 50 miles southeast of Orlando International Airport. As of 2026 it is described as the most productive cow-calf ranch in the United States.
summaries.Q3030287: A value resort at Walt Disney World, built on the unfinished half of the Pop Century Resort that was abandoned after the September 11 attacks. Its family suites opened on May 31, 2012, and standard rooms that September.
summaries.Q3030332: Disney's first timeshare property, opened on December 20, 1991, in Lake Buena Vista and renamed Old Key West in 1996. Its Key West-style rooms are the largest of any Disney Vacation Club resort, each with a kitchen.
summaries.Q3030339: A pair of connected hotels in Lake Buena Vista, French Quarter and Riverside, themed to New Orleans and the antebellum South. With more than 3,000 rooms between them, they form the largest resort by room count at Walt Disney World, linked to Disney Springs by the Sassagoula River.
summaries.Q3522110: A 32-story, 1,641-room resort hotel on International Drive, directly connected to the Orange County Convention Center. It now operates as the Hyatt Regency Orlando.
summaries.Q3565653: A resort hotel between EPCOT and Disney's Hollywood Studios, opened on January 13, 1990, and run by Marriott rather than Disney. It and its sister, the Dolphin, were designed by Michael Graves and are linked by a covered walkway across a lagoon.
summaries.Q39046636: A Disney Vacation Club resort between EPCOT and Disney's Hollywood Studios, opened on December 16, 2019, and served by the Disney Skyliner gondola. It is themed to Walt Disney's travels in Europe and the French and Italian Rivieras.
summaries.Q5079149: An art museum in Winter Park known for its Art Nouveau collection, including the most comprehensive collection of works by Louis Comfort Tiffany anywhere. It also holds American art pottery and late-19th and early-20th century American paintings and decorative arts.
summaries.Q2823492: A ghost town in eastern Lake County, settled in the late 19th century near Paisley. It is best known as the place where Walt Disney's parents, Flora and Elias Disney, lived for a short time after marrying in 1888, about 40 miles north of today's Walt Disney World.
summaries.Q2892164: A natural lake about a mile across and 35 feet deep at the north end of Walt Disney World, just east of Magic Kingdom. A water bridge links it to the Disney-made Seven Seas Lagoon.
summaries.Q3484003: A multi-purpose arena in Kissimmee with 8,300 seats, opened in 2003 at Osceola Heritage Park. It is home to the twice-yearly Silver Spurs Rodeo and also hosts concerts, family shows and graduations.
summaries.Q5061097: A 116-acre zoo and botanical garden in Sanford, north of Orlando, run as a not-for-profit focused on conservation. It has been accredited by the Association of Zoos and Aquariums since 1986.
summaries.Q24192030: An indoor family entertainment center on International Drive, opened in 2020 in a former shopping mall and run by developer Michael Dezer. Its main draw is the Orlando Auto Museum, with more than 2,000 vehicles, alongside arcades, go-karts, bowling and mini golf.
summaries.Q5282379: The inn at Disney's BoardWalk, a hotel and entertainment complex on Crescent Lake between EPCOT and Disney's Hollywood Studios, opened in 1996 and designed by Robert A.M. Stern Architects.
summaries.Q7028398: An all-suite hotel near Universal Orlando, about a mile from Walt Disney World, themed to Nickelodeon from 2005 to 2016. It has one- to three-bedroom suites and two water parks, the Lagoon Pool and the Oasis Pool.
summaries.Q3481157: A resort on Walt Disney World property owned by the U.S. Department of Defense and run as an Armed Forces Recreation Center for the military community. It was expanded between 2004 and 2006 and runs on non-appropriated funds, reinvesting all its profits.
summaries.Q66504185: A pair of value hotels at Universal Orlando, Surfside and Dockside, built on the former site of Wet 'n Wild. Surfside opened on June 27, 2019, and Dockside on December 15, 2020, themed to surfing and to a coastal retreat.
summaries.Q5671434: Tropical and semi-tropical gardens at 1920 North Forest Avenue in Orlando, with nearly 50 acres of landscaped grounds and lakes and trails shaded by 200-year-old oaks. A 15-acre section with the historic Leu House is a historic district.
summaries.Q6476049: A Florida state park north of Leesburg on Lake Griffin, linked by the Ocklawaha River to the Harris Chain of Lakes. Its 578 acres of swamp and upland hold one of the state's largest live oaks, and it is popular for boating, fishing, camping and wildlife viewing.
summaries.Q6476675: A 4,372-acre Florida state park south of Clermont, on the shore of Lake Louisa at the edge of the Green Swamp. Besides Lake Louisa it contains several smaller lakes among bald cypress, live oak and saw palmetto.
summaries.Q7354694: A 14,000-acre state reserve about 30 miles north of Orlando, with pine flatwoods, swamps, artesian springs and Indian mounds along Rock Springs Run and the Wekiva River. It is used for hiking, cycling, canoeing, horseback riding and wildlife viewing.
summaries.Q3364106: A 7,000-acre Florida state park in Apopka, about 20 minutes north of Orlando, at the headwaters of the Wekiva River. The springs use the Wekiwa spelling while the river and many nearby streets use Wekiva.
summaries.Q7751017: An art museum in Loch Haven Park in Orlando, in the former Howard Phillips house by Lake Formosa, opened on November 22, 1998. Its core is a collection of paintings by Earl Cunningham donated by Marilyn and Michael Mennello, and the city of Orlando runs it.
summaries.Q3352593: An interactive gallery at Disney's Hollywood Studios, opened on October 1, 2001, about Walt Disney's life and his company. It shows memorabilia from the Disney archives and a short film about Walt Disney.
summaries.Q5171521: The art museum on the Winter Park campus of Rollins College, formerly the Cornell Fine Arts Museum and the only teaching museum in the Orlando area. Its more than 5,000 objects range from antiquity to the present, including old master paintings and prints.
summaries.Q23994724: A family-run company with two amusement parks, in Orlando and Kissimmee, founded by John Arie Sr., whose first venture opened in Orlando in 1979. Its flagship park on International Drive opened in 1997 and grew by 10 acres and two roller coasters in 2013.
summaries.Q7749778: A two-level upscale indoor mall on Conroy Road near Interstate 4 and the north end of International Drive, opened in 2002. Its anchors are Macy's, Bloomingdale's and Neiman Marcus, and it is the third-largest mall in the Orlando area.
summaries.Q123153074: An outdoor shopping, dining, residential and entertainment complex on Walt Disney World land, with a Winter Garden address. Announced in 2007, it opened its first phase in 2021.
summaries.Q56290726: A shopping center in Orlando, opened in 1956, when it was the largest retail development in Florida. It grew over the decades with enclosed wings and department stores such as Jordan Marsh, Belk and Ivey's.
summaries.Q1800922: A spring-fed lake of about 7,000 acres west of the city of Eustis, part of the Harris Chain of Lakes. Waterways connect it to Lake Harris, Lake Dora and, through Lake Griffin and the Ocklawaha River, to the St. Johns River and the Atlantic.
summaries.Q1800942: A lake 31 miles northwest of Orlando and, at 13,788 acres, the largest lake entirely within Lake County. It belongs to the Harris Chain of Lakes, with Leesburg on its northwestern shore.
summaries.Q4732653: A freshwater lake in Osceola County known as the 'Headwaters of the Everglades'. Besides alligators, it holds largemouth bass, bluegill, bowfin, gar and redear sunfish.
summaries.Q6477143: An undeveloped lake of about 1,160 acres in Paisley, at the edge of the Ocala National Forest. A Boy Scout camp occupies its north shore, and there is no public access or boat ramp.
summaries.Q6478059: The largest lake in Osceola County, known as Lake Toho, covering 22,700 acres with a 42-mile shoreline. Its main inflow, Shingle Creek, rises in Orlando, and a canal links it to East Lake Tohopekaliga.
summaries.Q6476349: A spring-fed lake of about 335 acres in Lake County, Florida.
summaries.Q5303533: The historic core and central business district of Orlando, made up of neighborhoods such as Thornton Park, Parramore, South Eola around Lake Eola, and the Lake Eola Heights and Lake Cherokee historic districts.
summaries.Q6477133: A 17-square-mile planned community inside Orlando's city limits, southeast of Orlando International Airport, named for a large lake in its northern part.
summaries.Q5116717: Orlando's old railroad depot, built in 1889 by the South Florida Railroad and used for passenger trains until 1926. The depot and surrounding buildings now form a retail and entertainment center, with a SunRail stop.
summaries.Q7910651: A public college founded in 1968, with its main campus in Orlando and others across Orange and Osceola counties. It is part of the Florida College System and offers associate and bachelor's degrees.
summaries.Q21196867: A spring near Okahumpka with a 400-foot-wide pool about 170 feet deep, whose run flows north toward Lake Harris. The land was once a Seminole village site; since 2011 the whole property has belonged to the U.S. Navy.
summaries.Q5470927: A fort built during the Second Seminole War in what is now Christmas, Florida, begun on December 25, 1837, when about 2,000 U.S. Army soldiers and Alabama volunteers arrived.
summaries.Q19757453: A restaurant at Disney's Hollywood Studios that recreates a kitschy 1950s family kitchen. Servers act like the guests' mothers, even scolding diners who 'misbehave', while 1950s television plays.
summaries.Q19880295: A restaurant at Disney's Hollywood Studios, next to the 50's Prime Time Café, known for character meals. It is one of three restaurants in the park that offer early entry to the Fantasmic! show.
summaries.Q19880772: A restaurant in the France pavilion of EPCOT's World Showcase, which sits between the Morocco and United Kingdom pavilions.
summaries.Q30589703: A pub and dining room in the United Kingdom pavilion of EPCOT's World Showcase, which represents England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, between the France and Canada pavilions.
summaries.Q36418296: A restaurant in the Germany pavilion of EPCOT's World Showcase, between the China and Italy pavilions.
summaries.Q7754604: The entrance area of Disney's Animal Kingdom, with waterfalls, exotic plants and animals chosen for their gentle nature, so guests meet wildlife as soon as they arrive. Residents include giant anteaters, swamp wallabies, macaws and black swans.
summaries.Q4769423: A historic theater on the Rollins College campus in Winter Park, built in 1931 and named for the English-born actress Annie Russell. It was designed by Richard Kiehnel and listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1998.
summaries.Q5528860: A hotel and convention center in Kissimmee, opened on February 2, 2002, with 1,718 rooms and suites and 500,000 square feet of meeting space. It serves as Osceola County's de facto convention center.
summaries.Q6479106: A historic inn at 100 North Alexander Street in Mount Dora, built in 1883 as the ten-room Alexander House. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1987.
summaries.Q5282376: The Disney Vacation Club villas at Disney's Beach Club Resort, a New England-style resort on Crescent Lake in the EPCOT area of Walt Disney World, opened in 1990.
summaries.Q5282377: The Disney Vacation Club villas at Disney's BoardWalk, a hotel and entertainment complex on Crescent Lake between EPCOT and Disney's Hollywood Studios, opened in 1996.
summaries.Q6674526: A historic hotel in Longwood, built in 1885 and also known as the St. George Hotel, later moved from Old Dixie Highway to 300 North Ronald Reagan Boulevard. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1984.
summaries.Q6772968: A Marriott Vacation Club timeshare resort on International Drive and the largest in its portfolio, with 1,616 studios and villas in 24 Mission-style buildings.
summaries.Q6772974: A large hotel and convention center near Walt Disney World, on World Center Drive, a road renamed after the resort when International Drive was extended south.
summaries.Q2002896: A Disney Vacation Club tower beside Disney's Contemporary Resort, opened in 2009 between Bay Lake and Magic Kingdom. It shares the Contemporary's theme and stands where the old North Garden Wing once was.
summaries.Q2049010: A 394-room hotel on Walt Disney World property at 1850 Hotel Plaza Boulevard, across from Disney Springs.
summaries.Q3266490: A 323-room hotel on Hotel Plaza Boulevard in Lake Buena Vista, on Walt Disney World property near Disney Springs, with views over the resort from some rooms.
summaries.Q2417065: A resort hotel on Walt Disney World property in Lake Buena Vista, across from Disney Springs.
summaries.Q2667158: A business and convention hotel next to Disney Springs, opened on November 23, 1983, on Walt Disney World property but not run by Disney. It has 787 rooms and 27 suites, many overlooking Disney Springs.
summaries.Q2717781: Disney Vacation Club villas at Disney's Wilderness Lodge, a lodge-style resort on Bay Lake near Magic Kingdom that opened on May 28, 1994. The Boulder Ridge Villas, the first of two villa sections, opened in 2000.
summaries.Q7981040: The former Wells'Built Hotel in Orlando's historic Parramore district, built by Dr. William Monroe Wells for African American travelers during segregation, when it hosted many now-famous Black performers. It is now an African American history museum and has been on the National Register since 2000.
summaries.Q14686335: A two-story red-brick building in Sanford, built in 1886–1887 for Henry B. Plant to serve travelers arriving on his railroad and steamship lines. Architect William T. Cotter designed it in Romanesque and Moorish Revival styles.
summaries.Q4985460: A 1,011-room Hilton resort on 27 acres directly across from Disney Springs, opened on March 10, 1983. It is linked to Disney Springs by pedestrian skybridges.
summaries.Q5531967: A paved rail trail and Florida state park following 29 miles of an abandoned Seaboard Air Line Railroad line through the Green Swamp, from Polk City to Mabel. It is named for General James A. Van Fleet, a commander in both World Wars and the Korean War.
summaries.Q6693891: An 18,000-acre Florida state park along six miles of the St. Johns River in Lake and Seminole counties. It forms a wildlife corridor to the Ocala National Forest along the Wekiva and St. Johns rivers.
summaries.Q7099581: A non-profit history museum in the historic Orange County Courthouse in downtown Orlando. Its five floors of exhibits trace local and regional history from 2,000 years ago to today.
summaries.Q7103184: A private science museum in Orlando that teaches science and technology through hands-on experiences. It is accredited by the American Alliance of Museums.
summaries.Q6516441: A museum of local history at 111 South Sixth Street in Leesburg, in a building put up in 1922 by the Leesburg Woman's Club.
summaries.Q6920473: An arts center at 847 East Fifth Avenue in Mount Dora that runs classes, workshops, gallery shows and children's programs. Its annual arts festival in February draws more than 200,000 visitors to the town.
summaries.Q8031719: A science-themed entertainment center on International Drive, part of a small chain whose buildings look as if they were placed upside down. Its many hands-on exhibits mix education and entertainment.
summaries.Q6920474: A local history museum at 450 Royellou Lane in Mount Dora, in a 1920s building that was once the city's firehouse and jail.
summaries.Q6941069: A local history museum at 122 East Fifth Street in Apopka, run by the Apopka Historical Society, with exhibits on the town and the pioneers of northwest Orange County.
summaries.Q5061094: A railroad museum in a 1913 Tavares and Gulf depot at 101 South Boyd Street in Winter Garden, opened in 1983. It covers Central Florida's railroad history and has a large collection of dining-car china.
summaries.Q16908806: A local history museum in Lady Lake, in a building first put up by the Atlantic Coast Line Railroad. Its exhibits include citrus-industry artifacts, a model railroad, tools and photographs.
summaries.Q16920165: A museum and arts center in Maitland, formed in 2010 by merging the Maitland Art Center, known for its artists' bungalow colony and a National Historic Landmark, with the local historical society. It also runs small telephone, house and carpentry museums.
summaries.Q16947169: A local history museum in a former railroad freight depot in Winter Park, run by the Winter Park Historical Association. Its exhibits cover local schools, railroads, the turpentine industry and the town's past businesses.
summaries.Q96393959: A house museum in Eatonville, built in 1888 and the town's second-oldest building. Author Zora Neale Hurston often visited her friend Matilda Moseley here; restored, it opened as a museum in 2000.
summaries.Q6475803: An art museum opened in 1995, the first in Lake County devoted entirely to visual art. It shows historic and contemporary work from local, regional and national artists.
summaries.Q17060840: An art museum in Eatonville named for Zora Neale Hurston, the writer and folklorist who grew up in the town. Its changing exhibitions focus on artists of African descent.
summaries.Q21016305: A fine-dining restaurant in Disney's Grand Floridian Resort & Spa, opened in 1988 and named for Queen Victoria and Prince Albert. Its menu changes with the seasons.
summaries.Q109283648: A restaurant in Frontierland at Magic Kingdom, the themed land modeled on the 19th-century American frontier of cowboys, saloons and gold rushes.
summaries.Q16947265: An outdoor shopping center at 9101 International Drive, next to the Orange County Convention Center.
summaries.Q30589790: A restaurant in the Italy pavilion of EPCOT's World Showcase, between the Germany pavilion and The American Adventure.
summaries.Q36417129: A restaurant in Liberty Square at Magic Kingdom, the land themed to colonial America, with replicas of the Liberty Bell and Liberty Tree, the Haunted Mansion and the Hall of Presidents.
summaries.Q108853180: A space-themed restaurant at EPCOT, opened on September 20, 2021. Diners ride a simulated space elevator 220 miles up to a station with views of Earth, and the menu is modern American.
summaries.Q7976182: A historic theater at 201 South Magnolia Avenue in Sanford, also known as the Ritz or Milane Theatre and listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2001. It was renamed for donor Wayne Densch.
summaries.Q7757474: One of Orlando's oldest theaters, turned from a cinema into a theater and then a music venue. It has a main hall and a smaller second room, and hosts both local shows and national acts.
summaries.Q7863952: A 2,000-seat stadium on the UCF main campus, home to the Knights' track and field, cross country and soccer teams.
summaries.Q4736134: A two-story mall in Altamonte Springs near Interstate 4 and State Road 436, anchored by Dillard's, JCPenney, Macy's and an AMC multiplex. It is the largest enclosed mall in Seminole County.
summaries.Q7103084: A two-story indoor mall in Orlando, opened in 1973, with anchors including Macy's. Several former anchors, such as Sears and JCPenney, have closed.
summaries.Q7734514: A large mall south of Orlando at Orange Blossom Trail and Sand Lake Road, opened in 1986. Its anchors include Dillard's, Macy's, JCPenney and the Crayola Experience.
summaries.Q6422416: An athletic village and shopping center on the UCF main campus, with housing for more than 2,000 students, shops and restaurants, the 10,000-seat Addition Financial Arena and the smaller Venue at UCF.
summaries.Q7986106: A single-level mall in Ocoee, west of Orlando, opened in 1996 at Colonial Drive and Clarke Road. It has 125 store spaces and anchors such as JCPenney and an AMC theater.
summaries.Q41910740: An outdoor shopping center in Winter Park, opened in 1999 on the site of the old Winter Park Mall. It has a 20-screen cinema, shops such as REI and Publix, and restaurants.
summaries.Q21020907: A park in downtown Orlando, created in 1991 beside Greenwood Cemetery, that serves as a home for many animal species.
summaries.Q28209839: A county nature preserve on the shore of Lake Butler, southwest of Orlando, managed by Orange County Parks and Recreation.
summaries.Q64784316: A 25-acre park on Kissimmee's waterfront near the historic downtown, on Lake Tohopekaliga. It has a 1.1-mile lakeside trail, event spaces, playgrounds, splash pads and fishing piers.
summaries.Q5773654: A baseball stadium in Sanford near Lake Monroe, built in 1951 as the New York Giants' spring training ground on the site of a 1926 field. Babe Ruth, Jackie Robinson and Willie Mays are among the stars who played there.
summaries.Q4721947: A baseball stadium in Winter Park, home to the Rollins College baseball and softball teams, on land donated to the city in 1926. It is named for Rollins booster Harold Alfond.
summaries.Q6166393: The baseball stadium of the UCF Knights on the university's main campus, formerly called Jay Bergman Field.
summaries.Q7144074: A 2,000-seat baseball stadium in Leesburg's Venetian Gardens on the shore of Lake Harris. It was the first lighted baseball stadium in Florida and hosted several minor-league teams and spring training camps.
summaries.Q5304324: Orlando's main performing arts center, in downtown, which opened on November 6, 2014. It joined the older Bob Carr Theater, opened in 1927 as the Orlando Municipal Auditorium, as the city's main stage.
summaries.Q8688: The main airport of the San Francisco Bay Area, about 12 miles southeast of the city in San Mateo County but owned by the City and County of San Francisco. It is the second-busiest airport in California, after LAX.
summaries.Q180615: A live-performance theater on Hollywood Boulevard and Highland Avenue, opened on November 9, 2001, as the Kodak Theatre. It has hosted the Academy Awards every year since then.
summaries.Q19520501: An indoor stadium in Inglewood on the former Hollywood Park racetrack site, opened in September 2020 under a translucent roof. It seats about 70,000, is home to the NFL's Rams and Chargers, and hosted Super Bowl LVI in 2022.
summaries.Q129421: A public research university in Davis, the northernmost of the ten University of California campuses. Founded in 1905 as an agricultural branch, it became a full campus in 1959 and now also teaches medicine, law, engineering and veterinary medicine.
summaries.Q864339: A stadium in Miami Gardens, home of the NFL's Miami Dolphins and the University of Miami Hurricanes. It has hosted six Super Bowls, two World Series and several national championship games.
summaries.Q1058864: A Houston stadium that opened in 2002 as the first NFL venue with a retractable roof, seating about 72,000. It is home to the Houston Texans and the Houston Livestock Show and Rodeo, and hosted Super Bowls in 2004 and 2017.
summaries.Q127530: The main international airport for Miami, about 6 miles west-northwest of downtown, historically known as Wilcox Field. It has more than 1,000 daily flights to 195 destinations, including most of Central and South America and the Caribbean.
summaries.Q670897: A public research university in Tempe, founded in 1885 as the Territorial Normal School to train teachers. It is now one of the largest public universities in the U.S. by enrollment.
summaries.Q305949: A national park in northeastern Arizona named for its large deposits of petrified wood, covering about 346 square miles of colorful badlands and semi-desert. Interstate 40 and historic Route 66 cross it, and its northern part reaches into the Painted Desert.
summaries.Q744748: Houston's main international airport, about 23 miles north of downtown, opened in 1969 as Houston Intercontinental. It was renamed in 1997 for President George H. W. Bush, a Houston resident.
summaries.Q29247: A hilltop campus of the Getty Museum in Brentwood, Los Angeles, opened on December 16, 1997, and known for its architecture, gardens and views over the city. Visitors ride a small hovertrain from the parking garage, and it draws about 1.8 million visitors a year.
summaries.Q731126: An art museum in Los Angeles on two campuses, the Getty Center and the Getty Villa, run by the J. Paul Getty Trust. The Center shows European paintings, drawings, manuscripts, sculpture and decorative arts made before 1900, as well as photographs.
summaries.Q1047293: A public research university on 2,001 acres of forested hills above Monterey Bay, one of the ten University of California campuses. About 20,000 students study in its ten residential colleges.
summaries.Q849784: A stadium in Exposition Park, Los Angeles, completed in 1923 as a memorial to the city's World War I veterans. Home of the USC Trojans football team, it seated more than 100,000 people for decades.
